Hack Tracker
https://hacktracking.com/
Last updated: November 18, 2026

What counts as hacking:
Internet hacking is the unauthorized access, manipulation, or exploitation of digital devices, computer systems, and network connections. It happens when someone finds and uses a weakness in software, hardware, or human behavior to steal data, disrupt services, or take control of a system.

Confirmed Hacks were confirmed by the affected organization, a government agency, or law enforcement. Numbers come from those statements, filings, or the linked reporting. Attacker claims are labeled as claims.

Speculated / Potential Hacks are outages or incidents where the public wondered about a hack. They are not confirmed hacks. Each one shows what the organization or investigators officially said.

The list is reviewed and updated about every two hours during the day, Eastern Time. Sorted by scale and impact, biggest first. Severity is a rough editorial rating, not an official score. Covers roughly the past 12 months, plus a few older events that are still widely referenced.

CONFIRMED HACKS

1. Binance (crypto exchange)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#binance-2026-10
   Date: Oct 29, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Finance, Crypto
   Summary: Hackers drained about $6.3 billion in crypto from Binance's hot wallets, the largest crypto theft on record. Blockchain analysts traced it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.
   Impact: About $6.3 billion stolen. Binance says it covered all losses and resumed withdrawals.
   Status: Confirmed by Binance. Losses covered.
   Sources:
     - Binance announcement: https://www.binance.com/en/support/announcement/detail/c5a8729a97ac486d963784d96c5642d7
     - CNBC: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/31/binance-hack-asset-coverage-withdrawals.html
     - Chainalysis: https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/binance-exploit-latest-findings-and-response/

2. Instructure (Canvas learning platform)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#instructure-2026-05
   Date: May 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Education, Tech
   Summary: The ShinyHunters gang stole data from Canvas, the school platform used by thousands of schools and universities, then defaced login pages during finals. Instructure later reached an agreement with the hackers.
   Impact: Names, emails, student IDs and some private messages. Hackers claimed 275 million users; TechCrunch reported more than 30 million students and staff.
   Status: Confirmed by Instructure.
   Sources:
     - BleepingComputer: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/instructure-confirms-data-breach-shinyhunters-claims-attack/
     - TechCrunch: https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/07/hackers-deface-school-login-pages-after-claiming-another-instructure-hack/
     - Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/canvas-parent-company-reaches-agreement-with-hacking-group-behind-recent-breach-2026-05-12/

3. FBI surveillance system
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#fbi-surveillance-system-2026-04
   Date: April 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Government
   Summary: The FBI declared a "major cyber incident" and notified Congress after a suspected China-linked breach of a system tied to wiretaps and surveillance targets.
   Impact: Possible exposure of surveillance-target information; full scope not disclosed.
   Status: Confirmed by the FBI. Investigation ongoing.
   Sources:
     - POLITICO: https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/01/fbi-hack-surveillance-system-major-incident-00854237
     - NBC News: https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/fbi-labels-suspected-china-hack-law-enforcement-data-major-cyber-incid-rcna266495

4. Stryker (medical technology)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#stryker-2026-03
   Date: Mar 11, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Healthcare, Manufacturing
   Summary: Iran-linked hackers (Handala) took over admin accounts and remotely wiped tens of thousands of company devices, disrupting operations for weeks.
   Impact: Roughly 80,000 devices wiped (BleepingComputer); fully operational again about three weeks later.
   Status: Confirmed by Stryker. Recovered.
   Sources:
     - BleepingComputer: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/medtech-giant-stryker-fully-operational-after-data-wiping-attack/
     - Krebs on Security: https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/03/iran-backed-hackers-claim-wiper-attack-on-medtech-firm-stryker/

5. ConnectWise (IT management software)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#connectwise-2026-10
   Date: October 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech
   Summary: Chinese state-linked hackers stole credentials from ConnectWise's cloud backup service and used them to get into customers' Microsoft 365 accounts, spying on thousands of companies.
   Impact: Customer Microsoft 365 tenants (email and files) potentially accessed; Cloud Backup taken offline.
   Status: Confirmed by ConnectWise and Microsoft.
   Sources:
     - TechCrunch: https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/22/chinese-hackers-spied-on-thousands-of-companies-after-breaching-it-giant-connectwise/
     - The Hacker News: https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/connectwise-resets-credentials-as-cloud.html

6. Expedia Group (travel)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#expedia-group-2026-11
   Date: Nov 12, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Travel, Consumer, Tech
   Summary: Expedia Group, owner of Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo, confirmed attackers reached its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider in a supply chain attack that hit several companies. The n0n extortion group claims it stole more than 1 TB of Expedia data. Security researchers had described a similar attack using access tied to the Qubole data platform; Expedia has not named the vendor.
   Impact: Not disclosed by Expedia. n0n claims (unverified) hundreds of millions of account records and about 830 million rows of loyalty program data, plus traveler profiles and trip records.
   Status: Breach confirmed by Expedia. Scale and n0n's data claims unconfirmed; investigation ongoing.
   Sources:
     - Skift: https://skift.com/2026/11/12/expedia-confirms-cyberattack-through-third-party-vendor/
     - Security Affairs: https://securityaffairs.com/203062/cyber-crime/extortion-group-claims-theft-of-nearly-one-billion-expedia-traveler-records.html

7. Optimizely (website experimentation platform)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#optimizely-2026-11
   Date: Nov 16, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech, Retail, Finance
   Summary: Attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into scripts that run on customers' websites. Researchers at Report URI found the code on 178 organizations' sites, including big names like Salesforce, Zoom, HSBC, CNN and Ikea, so visitors to those sites were exposed without the companies themselves being breached.
   Impact: Per Report URI, the malware swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and tried to deliver iOS exploit kits to iPhones and iPads; at least $7,000 in crypto was traced as stolen. Most of the malicious code was removed the same day.
   Status: Confirmed by Optimizely. In a Nov. 18 update it said under 5% of its customers were affected, the flaw (in its Web Experimentation sign-up flow) was closed within three hours of detection, and all injected code has been removed.
   Sources:
     - The Record: https://therecord.media/optimizely-malicious-code-customer-sites
     - TechTarget: https://www.techtarget.com/news/optimizely-supply-chain-attack-turns-trusted-scripts-against-178-orgs/874997/
     - Security Today: https://securitytoday.com/articles/2026/11/18/optimizely-patches-signup-flaw-after-attackers-inject-malicious-code.aspx

8. PLAID KARTE customers (MUFG Bank, JINS, Shimamura and others, Japan)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#plaid-karte-customers-2026-11
   Date: Nov 13, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech, Finance, Retail
   Summary: Attackers exploited a vulnerability in servers run by PLAID, the Tokyo company behind the KARTE customer-data marketing service, stole credentials used to connect to its systems and databases, and read data out. They also took over a PLAID account to get into the admin console. PLAID shut down all KARTE services on Nov. 13, and companies that use KARTE have been announcing leaks of their own customers' data since.
   Impact: Varies by company. MUFG Bank: about 6.5 million records of gender, age and region (no names or contact details). JINS: up to about 18.29 million accounts (email, surname, birth date and more). Shimamura: about 7 million members' birth dates, gender, prefecture and postal code. RIZAP: up to about 4.32 million email addresses. J.League: about 2.38 million ticketing records (internal user IDs, birth dates, gender, prefecture and city). Stripe International: about 150,000 STRIPE CLUB records with email addresses and member IDs. PLAID also says credentials used to link KARTE to outside services leaked, and has asked customers to revoke them.
   Status: Confirmed by PLAID and affected companies. KARTE still offline with no restart date as of Nov. 18.
   Sources:
     - MUFG Bank notice (Japanese, PDF): https://www.bk.mufg.jp/news/news2026/pdf/news1118.pdf
     - ITmedia NEWS (Japanese): https://www.itmedia.co.jp/news/article/2611/18/2000003287/
     - J.League notice (Japanese): https://www.jleague.jp/news/article/35384/

9. Rakuten Securities (online brokerage, Japan)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#rakuten-securities-2026-11
   Date: Nov 11, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Finance
   Summary: Attackers got into a test-environment system at Rakuten Securities on Nov. 11 and customer data held there may have been taken. The company detected the intrusion on Nov. 16 and blocked it.
   Impact: Login IDs and customer codes for up to about 11.25 million accounts; names, birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, emails, employers, withdrawal bank accounts, and self-reported income and assets for up to about 4.47 million accounts. Rakuten says passwords and PINs were not leaked and no unauthorized trades have been found.
   Status: Confirmed by Rakuten Securities. Investigation ongoing.
   Sources:
     - Rakuten Securities announcement (Japanese): https://www.rakuten-sec.co.jp/web/company/newsrelease/pdf/press2026111702.pdf
     - The Japan Times: https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/2026/11/18/companies/rakuten-securities-unauthorized-access/
     - NHK World: https://www3.nhk.or.jp/nhkworld/news/20261117de77429/

10. DHC (cosmetics, Japan, via PLAID KARTE)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#dhc-2026-11
   Date: Nov 13, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Retail, Consumer
   Summary: Unauthorized access to KARTE, a marketing service run by PLAID that DHC used for direct mail and similar messages, leaked DHC customer account information linked to it. PLAID notified DHC on Nov. 13.
   Impact: About 19.11 million customer account records (names, email addresses, birth dates and more). DHC says online-shop passwords and card data were not included and no secondary damage has been confirmed.
   Status: Confirmed by DHC. Regulator to be notified.
   Sources:
     - Nikkei (Japanese): https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXZQOUC1886Z0Y6A111C2000000/

11. DentaQuest (dental benefits)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#dentaquest-2026-05
   Date: May 17, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Healthcare
   Summary: Hackers were inside DentaQuest's network for several days and stole personal and health data. It is the largest healthcare breach reported to U.S. regulators this year.
   Impact: 15 million people (HHS filing).
   Status: Confirmed. Notices sent.
   Sources:
     - Healthcare Dive: https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/Dental-benefits-administrator-discloses-breach/827533/

   Date: Oct 28, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech, Consumer
   Summary: Attackers broke into a Japanese newsletter service used by hundreds of brands, including SEGA, and took subscriber email lists.
   Impact: 81,329,467 email addresses from up to about 380 client companies (company count; addresses, not people).
   Status: Confirmed by ARARA. Investigation ongoing.

14. IDScan.net (ID verification)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#idscan-net-2026-09
   Date: Sept 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech, Consumer
   Summary: A company that scans driver's licenses for bars, stores and other businesses confirmed hackers copied ID data from its cloud. Hackers advertised photos of more than 150 million North American drivers.
   Impact: 13 million people per a state filing; hackers claimed about 153 million records.
   Status: Confirmed by IDScan.net.
   Sources:
     - TechCrunch: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/10/id-verification-giant-idscan-confirms-data-breach-with-more-than-150-million-drivers-licenses-stolen/

15. European Commission cloud
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#european-commission-cloud-2026-03
   Date: 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Government
   Summary: Hackers poisoned an update of Trivy, a popular security tool, to steal a European Commission cloud key, then took data from its cloud accounts.
   Impact: About 340 GB of data, including personal data and email content; data of 30 EU entities exposed (CERT-EU).
   Status: Confirmed by CERT-EU and the Commission.
   Sources:
     - CERT-EU: https://cert.europa.eu/blog/european-commission-cloud-breach-trivy-supply-chain

16. Poland's energy sector
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#poland-s-energy-sector-2025-12
   Date: Dec 29, 2025
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Energy, Government
   Summary: A coordinated, destructive attack hit more than 30 wind and solar farms and a major combined heat and power plant. Poland's CERT linked it to Russian state hackers.
   Impact: Communications disrupted at some grid connection points; power and heat generation did not stop.
   Status: Confirmed by CERT Polska and the Polish government.
   Sources:
     - CERT Polska report: https://cert.pl/en/posts/2026/01/incident-report-energy-sector-2025/

17. U.S. water systems (Iran-linked)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#u-s-water-systems-2026-04
   Date: 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Utilities, Government
   Summary: U.S. agencies warned that Iran-affiliated hackers were breaking into internet-exposed control equipment (PLCs) at water and wastewater systems and other critical infrastructure, causing operational disruption.
   Impact: Operational disruption at affected utilities; no single total published.
   Status: Confirmed by CISA, FBI, EPA and NSA advisories.
   Sources:

18. Equinor (energy company, Norway)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#equinor-2026-11
   Date: Nov 17, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Energy
   Summary: Norway's state-controlled oil and gas giant said it detected an ongoing cyberattack against some of its IT systems and was working to neutralise it.
   Impact: Some IT systems affected; staff may have trouble reaching corporate apps and IT services. Equinor says there are no indications data was stolen, the attack did not involve a computer virus, and oil and gas production was not affected.
   Status: Confirmed by Equinor. Work to neutralise the attack and restore systems ongoing; Equinor says it is too early to say how long that will take.
   Sources:
     - Equinor statement: https://www.equinor.com/news/20261711-equinor-detected-cyber-attack
     - Reuters via Euronext: https://live.euronext.com/en/financial-news/norways-equinor-detects-ongoing-cyberattack-oil-and-gas-output-unaffected

19. Visa (via third-party provider)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#visa-2026-11
   Date: Nov 17, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Finance
   Summary: A new ransomware gang called n0n listed Visa on its leak site and set a 48-hour deadline to publish data it claims to have stolen. Visa confirmed an incident, but says it started at an unnamed third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.
   Impact: Visa says its own systems were not involved or impacted and there is no indication payment data such as card numbers was affected. What the gang claims to have taken has not been shown.
   Status: Third-party incident confirmed by Visa. Gang's data claims unverified.
   Sources:
     - Cybernews: https://cybernews.com/security/visa-jpmorgan-data-breach/
     - CISO Brief: https://cisobrief.com/visa-confirms-third-party-incident-as-n0n-ransomware-gang-also-lists-jpmorgan-chase/

20. Irish credit unions (via Wellington IT)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#irish-credit-unions-2026-10
   Date: Oct 6, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Finance
   Summary: An attacker exploited a flaw in the online banking platform Wellington IT provides to Irish credit unions and pulled saved payee records in early October. Credit unions were only told in mid-November.
   Impact: About 40 credit unions affected, roughly a quarter of the country's total. Saved payee names, IBANs, BICs, addresses and payment references potentially exposed. Officials say member balances were not accessed and no financial losses have been reported.
   Status: Confirmed by affected credit unions and Ireland's government. Flaw closed. Assessment ongoing.
   Sources:
     - RTÉ: https://www.rte.ie/news/2026/1118/1599645-credit-union-data-breach-assessed/
     - Irish Department of Finance: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-finance/press-releases/t%C3%A1naiste-and-minister-troy-comment-on-suspected-cybersecurity-incident-involving-credit-unions/
     - Galway Live: https://www.ireland-live.ie/west/galway-live/galway-credit-union-cyberattack-9358558

21. South Korea government email system
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#south-korea-government-email-system-2026-11
   Date: Nov 16, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Government
   Summary: South Korea's Ministry of the Interior and Safety said hackers got into the government's administrative email system by going through vulnerable local government networks and exploiting a flaw in its single sign-on (SSO) login system.
   Impact: Abnormal access to about 300 government email accounts found so far. The breach was reported to the privacy regulator and affected people were notified.
   Status: Confirmed by South Korea's government. Joint investigation with NIS and KISA ongoing.
   Sources:
     - SBS News: https://news.sbs.co.kr/english/article.do?news_id=N1008847830
     - Aju Press: https://www.ajupress.com/view/20261116133270131

22. Nitori (furniture retailer, Japan)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#nitori-2026-11
   Date: Nov 6, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Retail, Consumer
   Summary: Japan's biggest furniture chain found intruders in a company system and says customer and order records may have been stolen.
   Impact: Up to 37.62 million potentially affected records (names, contact details, dates of birth); Nitori says the count includes duplicates and is not the number of people. No passwords or card numbers.
   Status: Confirmed by Nitori, which says attackers extracted data through a vulnerability in an online-shop admin server. How much leaked is still undetermined.
   Sources:
     - BleepingComputer: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japanese-furniture-giant-nitori-says-hackers-stole-376m-customer-records/

23. Maersk (shipping)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#maersk-2026-11
   Date: Nov 11, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Transportation, Logistics
   Summary: The shipping giant confirmed that a threat actor breached a legacy system belonging to a company it previously acquired and stole data. The WhiteArmor ransomware group claimed the attack and threatened to release about 100GB of data, demanding $5 million (attacker's claim).
   Impact: Maersk says the incident is isolated to a local system, current evidence indicates no sensitive data was disclosed, and shipping operations are not disrupted.
   Status: Confirmed by Maersk. Investigation ongoing.
   Sources:
     - BleepingComputer: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/maersk-confirms-data-breach-as-whitearmor-ransomware-demands-5-million/

24. Port of Santos authority (Brazil)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#port-of-santos-authority-2026-11
   Date: Nov 6, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Transportation, Logistics, Government
   Summary: A cyberattack hit the Santos Port Authority (APS), the state-owned company that runs Brazil's largest port, knocking its online systems partly offline after a power outage at its headquarters. APS later confirmed a ransom demand. Brazil's Federal Police are investigating.
   Impact: Port authority systems partly down for days; operators reported delays and manual scheduling, arrival records and billing. Terminals and ship movements kept running. APS says it does not know whether data was accessed.
   Status: Confirmed by the port authority. Recovery ongoing; attacker not officially named.
   Sources:
     - Folha de S.Paulo: https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/internacional/en/business/2026/11/port-of-santos-confirms-cyberattack-says-it-does-not-know-whether-data-was-accessed-without-authorization.shtml
     - G1 (Portuguese): https://g1.globo.com/sp/santos-regiao/porto-mar/noticia/2026/11/12/porto-de-santos-confirma-pedido-de-resgate-apos-ataque-hacker-7percent-dos-dados-foram-recuperados.ghtml

25. Cisco SD-WAN zero-day attacks
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-2026-02
   Date: Feb 25, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Tech, Government
   Summary: Attackers exploited unknown flaws in Cisco's SD-WAN network gear to get admin control. CISA ordered federal agencies to patch within two days and hunt for intruders.
   Impact: Unknown number of networks; Cisco Talos said the campaign went back to at least 2023.
   Status: Confirmed by Cisco and CISA (Emergency Directive 26-03).

30. IDC Frontier cloud (Japan)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#idc-frontier-cloud-2026-10
   Date: Oct 7, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Tech, Government
   Summary: Ransomware hit a SoftBank-group cloud provider, encrypting customer virtual servers used by companies and local governments.
   Impact: 495 companies and local governments disrupted.

SPECULATED / POTENTIAL HACKS

1. FAA: nationwide ground stop
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#faa-nationwide-ground-stop-2026-11
   Date: Nov 13, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Aviation, Government
   Summary: The FAA halted departures across the U.S. for more than four hours after its air traffic communications network became unstable. It came one day after the big Microsoft outage, so many people asked whether the two were linked or whether someone had hacked the system.
   What people speculated: A hack or coordinated attack on air traffic control, possibly connected to the Microsoft outage the day before.
   Official explanation: The FAA says it has "no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor." Its explanation: after a contractor installed a new router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, data flooded the FAA's legacy network (with a second problem site in Amarillo, Texas). Officials said it was not related to the Microsoft outage.
   Impact: Instability at 17 of 22 en route air traffic control centers; about 12,462 flights canceled that day (FAA figure).
   Status: No evidence of a hack. Root-cause investigation ongoing.
   Sources:
     - FAA: Nationwide Ground Stop Q&A: https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/nationwide-ground-stop-questions-and-answers
     - SecurityWeek: https://www.securityweek.com/no-signs-of-hacking-in-faa-ground-stop-as-fbi-reportedly-probes-software-update/
     - AP News: https://apnews.com/article/nationwide-ground-stop-trump-air-travel-faa-a638c9651f1fabe8f95d20353779ee5b

2. Microsoft 365 / Outlook global outage
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#microsoft-365-outlook-global-outage-2026-11
   Date: Nov 12, 2026
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech
   Summary: Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services went down worldwide for most of a business day, one of the largest outages in the company's history. Microsoft publicly pushed back on speculation that it had been hacked.
   What people speculated: A cyberattack on Microsoft's cloud.
   Official explanation: Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report calls it "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents": a hidden bug from a July update, extra traffic after a Teams failover, and about 14% of gateway servers already offline combined to freeze its gateway servers.
   Impact: At the worst point more than 80% of the affected gateway servers stopped responding; it took nearly 24 hours to stabilize email.
   Status: Official cause published. Not a hack.
   Sources:
     - Ars Technica: https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/microsoft-details-how-three-problems-combined-for-a-global-outage/
     - BleepingComputer: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/microsoft-says-months-old-bug-caused-global-microsoft-365-outage/
     - USA Today: https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/2026/11/13/microsoft-dismisses-cyberattack-speculation-amid-outage/92759759007/

3. CrowdStrike / Windows global IT outage
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#crowdstrike-windows-global-it-outage-2024-07
   Date: Jul 19, 2024
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech, Aviation
   Summary: A single update from security company CrowdStrike crashed Windows computers around the world, grounding flights and knocking banks, hospitals and broadcasters offline. It is still the go-to comparison whenever a big outage hits.
   What people speculated: A global cyberattack.
   Official explanation: CrowdStrike said the same day it was not a cyberattack. A faulty content update for its Falcon sensor caused Windows machines to crash.
   Impact: About 8.5 million Windows devices (Microsoft estimate).
   Status: Official cause published. Not a hack. (Older event, still widely referenced.)
   Sources:
     - CrowdStrike technical details: https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/falcon-update-for-windows-hosts-technical-details/
     - Microsoft: https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2024/07/20/helping-our-customers-through-the-crowdstrike-outage/

4. Amazon Web Services (US-EAST-1)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#amazon-web-services-2025-10
   Date: Oct 20, 2025
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Tech
   Summary: A failure in Amazon's biggest cloud region took down a long list of apps and websites for hours, leading many people to wonder if it was an attack on internet infrastructure.
   What people speculated: A cyberattack or DNS hijacking.
   Official explanation: AWS traced it to a hidden race condition in DynamoDB's automated DNS management that left a key DNS record empty. There was no sign of malicious activity.
   Impact: Widespread disruption to sites and apps that rely on AWS.
   Status: Official cause published. Not a hack.
   Sources:
     - BBC News: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cev1en9077ro
     - WIRED: https://www.wired.com/story/what-that-huge-aws-outage-reveals-about-the-internet/

5. Spain & Portugal blackout
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#spain-portugal-blackout-2025-04
   Date: Apr 28, 2025
   Severity: Critical
   Sectors: Energy, Government
   Summary: Nearly all of mainland Spain and Portugal lost power. In the first hours, a cyberattack was one of the theories openly discussed.
   What people speculated: A cyberattack on the power grid.
   Official explanation: Spain's government report (June 2025) and the European grid operators' expert panel final report (March 2026) found no evidence of a cyberattack. They blame voltage control problems and a chain of generator disconnections.
   Impact: Power cut across the Iberian Peninsula.
   Status: Official reports published. No cyberattack found. (Older event, final report in 2026.)
   Sources:
     - The Guardian: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/jun/17/expert-report-rules-out-cyber-attack-for-spain-and-portugal-april-blackout
     - ENTSO-E final report: https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/

6. Cloudflare global outage
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#cloudflare-global-outage-2025-11
   Date: Nov 18, 2025
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Tech
   Summary: Cloudflare, which sits in front of a huge share of websites, broke much of the web for several hours, including ChatGPT. Even Cloudflare's own team first suspected a massive DDoS attack.
   What people speculated: A huge DDoS (traffic-flood) attack.
   Official explanation: Cloudflare's postmortem says a database permission change made a configuration file for its bot-blocking system double in size, which crashed its core proxy software.
   Impact: Errors on a large share of websites using Cloudflare for several hours.
   Status: Official cause published. Not a hack.
   Sources:
     - Cloudflare postmortem: https://blog.cloudflare.com/18-november-2025-outage/
     - Ars Technica: https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2025/11/cloudflare-broke-much-of-the-internet-with-a-corrupted-bot-management-file/

7. Apple services outage (iCloud, App Store, Apple Pay)
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#apple-services-outage-2026-11
   Date: Nov 17, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Tech, Consumer
   Summary: iCloud sign-in, the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, AppleCare and Apple retail store systems went down for hours, the latest in a week of big U.S. outages.
   What people speculated: Another hit in a coordinated cyberattack behind the Microsoft, FAA, Chase and NSA outages.
   Official explanation: Apple said an internal update caused the outages and that it was not a cyberattack. The U.S. Director of National Intelligence also said the recent string of outages was not a cyberattack or a coordinated nation-state effort.
   Impact: Hours of sign-in failures and service outages; Apple stores unable to complete purchases. Services restored by that evening.
   Status: Company explanation given. Not a hack.
   Sources:
     - MacRumors: https://www.macrumors.com/2026/11/17/apple-outage-internal-update/
     - NBC News: https://www.nbcnews.com/business/corporations/apple-outages-working-get-systems-back-online-rcna609861

8. JPMorgan Chase online banking
   URL: https://hacktracking.com/#jpmorgan-chase-online-banking-2026-11
   Date: Nov 16, 2026
   Severity: High
   Sectors: Finance
   Summary: Chase's online banking slowed and transactions were delayed for hours, with knock-on delays at other banks. It was the fourth big U.S. outage in five days, which fed questions about a coordinated attack. On Nov 17 a new ransomware gang, n0n, listed JPMorgan Chase on its leak site, claiming it stole data; that is an unverified attacker claim.
   What people speculated: A cyberattack on the banking system, possibly linked to the Microsoft and FAA outages.
   Official explanation: Chase blamed a temporary software bug in on-premise hardware and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Asked about the gang's claim, the bank said there is no evidence linking the disruption to a cyberattack.
   Impact: Delayed transactions and online banking problems; some other banks affected when dealing with Chase.
   Status: Company explanation given. No evidence of a hack.
   Sources:
     - POLITICO: https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/16/jpmorgan-chase-banking-outage-software-bug-01168592
     - CNBC: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/jpmorgan-chase-technical-issue.html
